proposals.relationship: Armitage identifies Yates’s Art of Memory as the book that inspired his wish to write cultural and intellectual history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own retrospective account specifies a teenage reading and desired kind of history;not endorsement of every Yates thesis. First publication1966 and cited1978 reprint distinguished. The book itself remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage credits Skinner’s republicanism scholarship, supervision and sustained criticism with enabling his formation as an intellectual historian.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview identifies reading,matching republicanism interests and Cambridge transfer;own2000 acknowledgments separately name Skinner a reader,critic and interlocutor. No claim that administrative assistance alone proves doctrinal descent;Bock,Viroli and Russell Price retain the cited works’ editorial/translation credit. These works and dissertation remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage credits Pocock among his lasting intellectual inspirations during his Princeton fellowship.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2000 acknowledgment expressly distinguishes Princeton inspiration from later Cambridge questions and examination. Elliott,Lake,Quint and the other Princeton colleague retain plural credit. This narrow self-reported formative debt identifies no particular doctrine,book or sole supervisor;their works remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage credits Stone among his lasting intellectual inspirations during his Princeton fellowship.

proposals.relationship: Armitage credits Burke’s formative questions and support for a seminar connecting cultural and intellectual history with colonial encounters.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2000 acknowledgment credits Burke with Bayly,Collinson,Hont and Pagden;own2012 account specifies support for Cultural Encounters in the Early-Modern World,which Armitage organized with Joan-Pau Rubiés. Neither sole supervision nor a particular question is inferred.

proposals.relationship: Armitage describes his and Cannadine’s shared commitment to placing British history in imperial and wider international settings.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2012 account says their views on the field converged while Cannadine was taking his own imperial turn. This is a bounded comparison,not a claim that collegial generosity proves intellectual transmission or that the NACBS report was jointly authored by them. Cannadine’s Ornamentalism remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage credits conversations with Iriye and other international historians with helping crystallize his turn toward international and global history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2012 retrospective singles out the2000/1 Warren Center conversations and jointly credits Ernest May and James Kloppenberg. The resource is this intellectual exchange,not an unspecified Iriye book or sole conversion cause. It coexisted with Atlantic work.

proposals.relationship: Armitage explicitly acknowledges Bailyn’s expanding conception and seminars as an influence on his Atlantic historiography.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2012 answer to the named-influence question describes annual seminar participation1997–2005 and historiographical innovation. This is Armitage’s own retrospective attribution,not inference from appearing at Harvard;his parallel international turn and criticism of nationally bounded Atlantic histories remain explicit.
primary_locators: Interview2012,14–15,answers about national boundaries and Bailyn;27,note28.

proposals.relationship: Armitage identifies domestic and short-term limits in Skinner’s contextualism while crediting its achievements and later expansion toward longer historical spans.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2013 introduction3–4 specifies the international-actor omission,retaining the brief neo-Scholastic exception and period-wide context. Joint Guldi/Armitage2014,47–48,criticizes early synchronic narrowing but expressly credits Skinner’s late1990s longer-range studies as foreshadowing a broader return. Distinct qualified criticisms consolidate one pair/kind and coexist with acknowledged debt;neither all-contextualism rejection nor blanket claim about Skinner’s career follows. Skinner originals unread.
primary_locators: Joint Manifesto2014,frozen2October version,47–48/notes30–32,including late1990s return qualification.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Jo Guldi build their renewed longue-durée program on Braudel’s model while revising its treatment of change and agency.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint argument,not Armitage-only authorship. Frozen2October2014 PDF9–10 and15–17 distinguishes inheritance from a literal return;new data,flexibility and dynamism qualify the model. Braudel’s original1958 article/translation remain unread;later revised digital Manifesto is not substituted.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Bourdieu’s account of stylistic returns to explain why a renewed longue durée differs from its earlier form.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint2014 introduction explicitly applies this conceptual resource;no claim that Bourdieu advocated their historical program. The cited Field of Cultural Production essay remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Guldi draw on Eley’s account of the separation of local social histories from broader political and social explanation.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint2014 chapter uses Eley’s retrospective account and contrasts his ambitions with the separation he describes. This is their use of A Crooked Line,not independent confirmation that social history failed or agreement with every Eley argument. Full original book unread.
primary_locators: Manifesto2014,frozen2October version,39–45,especially45;135,note19 citing A Crooked Line184/129.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Ginzburg’s study of the benandanti as an example of microhistory operating across radically different temporal scales.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint2014 concession explicitly resists making microhistory intrinsically incompatible with temporal depth. The cited Storia notturna1989 is distinguished from his earlier benandanti book;neither original is freshly read.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Levi’s account of microhistory’s transformative capacity to qualify their criticism of its later anglophone practice.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint2014 quotation and attribution retain individual agency within constraining normative systems. This does not make Levi responsible for the book’s diagnosis of anglophone microhistory or identify him with the later practice criticized. His1991 chapter remains unread;Peter Burke is volume editor.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Hunt’s argument that the research question should determine scale to support synthesis between microhistory and macrohistory.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint2014 conclusion explicitly endorses Hunt’s qualification that mega-long-term history is not the only story. It coexists with Hunt’s later criticism of their project;does not imply her endorsement of their whole program. Writing History in the Global Era2014,120 is cited but unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Guldi present James C. Scott’s Zomia history as an example of combining local histories into an account that challenges inevitable state and economic development.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint2014 conclusion makes this specific methodological use of The Art of Not Being Governed2009. Scott’s historical claims are reported as their reading,not independently verified;no all-purpose influence or agreement is inferred. Original book unread.

proposals.relationship: Hunt disputes Armitage and Guldi’s diagnosis of historical short-termism and their treatment of cultural history and microhistory as causes of disciplinary crisis.
proposals.evidence_note: Fresh selected Portuguese translation by Danilo Alves Bezerra of Hunt’s2015 Annales response. Its direct target is their joint2015 Le retour de la longue durée article,not silently the whole2014 book. Hunt contests the data reading and treatment of Sewell,Davis,Darnton and Scott,and points to structural labor and educational changes;she also calls longue durée fruitful. French original and English edition were not read or paginated as this translation.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Guldi place Natalie Zemon Davis’s episodic cultural histories within their criticism of the narrowing horizons of anglophone microhistory.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint2014 chapter names the works as examples while conceding microhistory’s original ability to link scales,public popularity and critical gains. This does not say the author’s entire career lacked public engagement. Hunt’s2015 response expressly disputes the characterization;her target is the related2015 article. The cited Davis1975/Darnton1984 books remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage and Guldi place Joan Scott’s early labor history within a shift toward locally focused history that they argue weakened broader historical synthesis.
proposals.evidence_note: Joint2014 chapter50 names Glassworkers of Carmaux1974 alongside William Sewell,while conceding that close focus need not conflict with broad perspectives. This periodization critique is not rejection of Scott’s whole career. Hunt’s2015 reply disputes their treatment of Scott and emphasizes public interventions;the related2015 article itself remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage uses Weber’s analysis of charisma’s routinization and succession to suggest extensions to David A. Bell’s account of revolutionary leadership.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2021 review distinguishes Bell’s historical development of relational charisma from Weber’s theoretical resource,and offers friendly chronological,geographical and analytical amendments. Bell is not an available endpoint. This records Armitage’s actual use of Weber,not an arrow inferred from Bell’s own debt. Original Weber texts and Bell’s full book unread.

proposals.relationship: Armitage identifies the relation between charisma and race as a question left untreated by Weber’s account and Bell’s historical development of it.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2021review8 explicitly identifies the dual lacuna while inviting future investigation. This bounded conceptual criticism coexists with Armitage’s productive use of Weber and praise of Bell. It does not claim independent collation of Weber’s complete works or make Bell a graph endpoint;Chateaubriand supplies a historical illustration,not scholarly coauthorship.
